# Results — Study 458 (Abandoned-Baby / island-doji reversal)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **a doji
gapped away from both neighbours (an island) calls a reversal: buy the up-gap confirmation and
ride the turn** — encoded as a mechanical rule. A bullish abandoned baby is three bars: a
down candle in a decline, a **doji** (small body) that gaps **down** below it, and a
confirmation candle that gaps **up** above the doji and closes up. The pattern is confirmed on
the close of the confirmation bar (=t), entered at the **next close** (one documented lag), and
we measure the forward 5/10/20/60-day return. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Entries | **80** mechanical bullish abandoned babies pooled across the 5 tapes |
| Params | doji body ≤ **10%** of bar range; prior down-candle below its **SMA-20**; **body-gap** island (both sides) |
| Timing / costs | pattern confirmed on the close of bar C; enter the **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per trade |

> **Why the body-gap island, not the full-range island.** The strict "the doji's *entire* range
> sits below A's low and C's *entire* range sits above the doji's high" almost never fires on
> daily ETF data (a handful of entries in 21 years). The charitable mechanical encoding a
> proponent would accept gaps the *bodies* (open/close) — exactly the island a candlestick
> reader eyeballs. Even this looser version yields only **80** entries across 5 tapes — the
> pattern is genuinely rare, so every number here rides a thin sample.

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. The Signal axis uses a basket of **surviving** liquid ETFs; this is a
> single-instrument pattern study, not a cross-sectional anomaly, so survivorship affects only the
> drift baseline, which the random-entry control neutralizes.

## The signal — abandoned baby vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch pattern-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = pattern − random.

| horizon | n | pattern | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (patt−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 80 | +44.3 bps | 56% | +1.53 | +10.3 bps | +34.1 bps | +42.3 bps | +1.02 | 0.312 |
| 10-day | 80 | +88.4 bps | 60% | +2.29 | +53.6 bps | +34.9 bps | +86.4 bps | +0.71 | 0.478 |
| 20-day | 80 | +79.6 bps | 57% | +1.30 | +33.1 bps | +46.5 bps | +77.6 bps | +0.67 | 0.501 |
| 60-day | 80 | +407.2 bps | 75% | +3.54 | +118.9 bps | **+288.3 bps** | +405.2 bps | **+2.58** | **0.011** |

Read it carefully. Unlike most chart-tool teardowns, the pattern-minus-random delta is
**positive at every horizon**, and at **60 days** it clears the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar
(Welch *t* = +2.58, *p* = 0.011). That is a *weak* live signal, not a flat nothing. But it is
**not robust**: at 5/10/20 days the difference is nowhere near significant (Welch *t* ≤ 1.0),
the whole study rides **80 trades**, and — as the placebo and per-ticker tables below show —
the lone 60-day result does **not** trace to the island *geometry*. It is mostly the longest,
most drift-loaded horizon doing what long horizons do.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — no coherent cross-sectional island effect

| ticker | entries | pattern | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (patt−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 15 | +208.4 bps | +1.84 | +39.3 bps | **+169.1 bps** |
| QQQ | 13 | −170.6 bps | −1.24 | +88.2 bps | **−258.8 bps** |
| IWM | 13 | +74.3 bps | +0.67 | +2.7 bps | **+71.7 bps** |
| DIA | 17 | +299.5 bps | +2.19 | +33.7 bps | **+265.8 bps** |
| GLD | 22 | −27.3 bps | −0.26 | +1.5 bps | **−28.8 bps** |

The sign **flips across instruments** (SPY/DIA/IWM positive, QQQ/GLD negative) on 13–22 trades
each. That scatter — not a coherent edge across the board — is the hallmark of a thin,
luck-driven sample, not a real island-reversal mechanism.

## Geometry placebo — break the island, the result survives

The decisive "does the island's gap structure matter?" test: keep the same doji-after-a-decline
candidate pool and the same number of picks, but **strip the two-sided-gap requirement** and
draw the entries at random from the candidates — the island geometry is destroyed, the marginal
of three-bar windows is kept.

| test | observed pattern return | placebo *p* | candidates |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY gap-scramble, H = 20 | +208.4 bps | **0.307** | 104 |
| SPY gap-scramble, H = 60 | +684.9 bps | 0.070 | 104 |
| DIA gap-scramble, H = 60 | +780.5 bps | **0.018** | 120 |
| QQQ gap-scramble, H = 60 | +38.1 bps | 0.936 | 101 |
| IWM gap-scramble, H = 60 | +302.8 bps | 0.473 | 114 |
| GLD gap-scramble, H = 60 | +209.3 bps | 0.760 | 143 |

At H = 20 on SPY, **31% of gap-scrambled draws match or beat the real island** (*p* = 0.307):
the gaps are not load-bearing — a doji-after-a-decline picked at random does about as well.
At H = 60 the picture is incoherent: the geometry "matters" for DIA (*p* = 0.018) but is
useless for QQQ/IWM/GLD (*p* ≥ 0.47). There is **no consistent evidence the island gaps carry
the signal** — what little shows up traces to the doji-after-decline context plus drift.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real island bounce

On a deterministic tape with *planted* island bottoms (knob `edge`), the same abandoned-baby
rule behaves exactly as it must — so the thin real-tape result is a genuine "almost nothing
there", not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | pattern | win% | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no bounce) | 48 | −23.1 bps | 56% | −0.19 |
| **0.60** (real planted bounce) | 139 | +404.4 bps | 69% | **+5.96** |

With no planted bounce the control sits at *t* ≈ 0 (no false positive); a real planted island
bounce lights up at *t* = +5.96 with a 69% win-rate. The detector is live — so the weak,
horizon-isolated real-tape result is honest.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The abandoned baby's pattern-minus-random delta is positive at every
  horizon and clears *t* ≥ 2 at **60 days only** (Welch *t* = +2.58, *p* = 0.011) — a *weak*
  live signal, not a flat nothing. But 5/10/20-day deltas are insignificant (Welch *t* ≤ 1.0),
  the whole study rides **80 trades**, and the effect does not survive the geometry placebo.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** A 60-day-only, 80-trade, sign-flipping-by-instrument signal that
  costs barely dent is **not scalable**: you cannot build a deployable strategy on one horizon
  and ~16 trades per name across two decades. There is something there, but it is too thin and
  too horizon-specific to bank.
- **"Does the island doji forecast a turn?" — BUSTED.** The gap-scramble placebo leaves the
  SPY H = 20 result intact (*p* = 0.307) and the geometry "matters" in only 1 of 5 names at
  H = 60. The two defining **gaps** — the whole point of the *abandoned* baby — are **not**
  load-bearing. The doji-after-a-decline context plus drift, not the island itself, account for
  the weak signal. The island doji does **not** forecast the turn.
